summary: Specifies a way to carry MP3 audio in RTP packets that holds up better when packets are lost. It is an alternative to the format in RFC 2250. It was replaced by RFC 5219.

plainLanguage.summary: It packs music into packages so that if a few get lost on the way, the song still sounds okay.

questions: how to send mp3 over rtp with packet loss
subtitle: A loss-tolerant way to send MP3 audio over RTP

tldr.problem: RFC 2250's RTP payload format for MP3 audio is inefficient when packets are lost because MP3 frames contain back-pointers to earlier data, making frame boundaries unsuitable for RTP packets.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3119 rearranges MP3 frames into Application Data Units (ADUs) that can be decoded independently, preceded by size descriptors, and optionally interleaved to spread losses across the stream.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now send MP3 over RTP with much better tolerance for packet loss. RFC 5219 later provided an updated specification.

today: RFC 3119 was replaced by RFC 5219, which provides an updated specification for loss-tolerant MP3 RTP payload format.

sections.title: MP3 Frame Structure and the Problem
sections.content:
MP3 frames begin with a 4-byte MPEG header defining properties like layer, mode (mono/stereo), and frame size. After optional CRC, each frame contains a variable-length "side info" structure (9 to 32 bytes depending on MPEG version and mode), followed by encoded audio data. Crucially, each frame includes a main_data_begin back-pointer that tells the decoder where in earlier frames the data for this frame begins. This is called an Application Data Unit (ADU).

RFC 2250 places MP3 frame boundaries at RTP packet boundaries. When a packet is lost, the loss of that MP3 frame makes some data in previous and future frames useless, even if they arrive intact. This is inefficient. A better format would align RTP packets with ADU boundaries so that losing one packet does not corrupt other frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Music files are packed in a tricky way: each chunk says "the stuff I need starts way back here." So if you lose one chunk, you lose pieces of the ones before and after it too. This document repackages the music to avoid that problem.

sections.title: ADU Frames and Descriptors
sections.content:
An ADU frame contains the original MPEG header (with optional back-pointer replacement, see section 6), optional CRC, the side info structure, and the complete sequence of encoded audio data for one ADU (from the main_data_begin back-pointer to the start of the next frame's back-pointer). This is self-contained and decodable independently.

Each ADU in an RTP packet is preceded by a 1 or 2-byte ADU descriptor. The descriptor has a continuation flag (C bit): 0 for the start of an ADU, 1 if data is a continuation from a previous packet. A type flag (T bit) selects between 1-byte (6-bit size field) and 2-byte (14-bit size field) descriptors. Receivers must accept both sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each chunk (ADU) is labeled with its size and whether it continues from the previous packet. This label is 1 or 2 bytes depending on the chunk size.

sections.title: Packetization and Depacketization
sections.content: Packetization converts a sequence of MP3 frames into ADU frames, optionally interleaves them, then packs them into RTP packets. One or more ADU descriptor + ADU frame pairs fit in a packet if they fit completely; if a single ADU is too large, it spans multiple packets, with the first packet's descriptor having C=0 and continuation packets having C=1 (all with the same ADU size). Depacketization reverses this: receiving RTP packets are sorted by sequence number, ADUs are depacketized using the C flag to detect splits, and optionally deinterleaved and converted back to MP3 frames.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender groups chunks into network packets, and the receiver unpacks them, putting the chunks back in order.

sections.title: Handling Mixed Layers and Interleaving
sections.content:
MP3 files can mix layer III frames (which have back-pointers) with layer I or II frames (which are self-contained). When a mix is present, only layer III frames are converted to ADUs; layer I and II frames are sent with an ADU descriptor as-is. This allows the format to handle unusual cases.

Optional interleaving reuses the high-order 11 bits of the MPEG header (normally 0xFFE) as an Interleaving Sequence Number (ISN). The ISN is an 8-bit Interleave Index (within a cycle) plus a 3-bit Cycle Count. Senders can reorder ADUs before packetization to spread consecutive frames across non-consecutive packets, reducing the impact of burst losses. A receiving implementation must recognize and deinterleave ISNs; a sending implementation may omit interleaving (leaving 0xFFE). The RFC includes pseudo-code for both operations and example permutations.
sections.plainLanguage: If needed, the sender can shuffle chunks across packets using a hidden number in the header. This way, if several packets in a row are lost, the receiver still has pieces from different parts of the song.

sections.title: MIME Registration and SDP
sections.content: The MIME type is audio/mpa-robust. No parameters are required or optional. The encoding is defined only for RTP transport as specified in RFC 3119. This format is incompatible with audio/mpa and audio/mpeg MIME types. In SDP, the encoding name is mpa-robust. Example: m=audio 49000 RTP/AVP 121 with a=rtpmap:121 mpa-robust/90000. The RTP timestamp is in units of 1/90000 of a second, representing the presentation time of the first ADU in the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name is audio/mpa-robust. When you describe a session, you use 90,000 as the clock rate for timestamps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: If the session is encrypted and interleaving is used, the sender should ensure that any encryption key change coincides with the start of a new interleave cycle. Apart from this, the security considerations for this payload format are identical to those in RFC 2250. RTP security mechanisms apply as usual.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are scrambling the audio and shuffling chunks, keep encryption key changes and shuffle cycles in sync. Otherwise, the usual RTP security rules apply.
